gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a cold EV can use the plug-in power to keep its own pack warm instead of storing it: Tesla's manual says that when plugged in, the car 'uses the charging system, rather than the Battery itself, to keep your Battery warm'. InsideEVs reported that a Model 3 at -15 °F on a 9 A Level 1 cord for 14 hours gained only 1.14 kWh, about 7% of what the outlet supplied. At that rate a 2–3 kWh power station would add well under 1 mile in deep cold.
standout_why: I read the cited Jackery FAQ and the cited ryzzun.com page (dated 2026-10-23). Both cover grounding thoroughly: floating ground, the EV charger's ground-continuity check, the relay opening, Jackery's Grounding Adapter and Anker's EV mode. So the grounding problem is already taken (standout 0 on its own). The only thing ryzzun says about loss inside the car is 'Slow 120V charging tends to lose a bit more to the car's electronics staying awake.' Neither page says that a cold pack can take most of a Level 1 session for heating. ChatGPT's answer allows for a 15–25% loss and says cold only shortens the drive, not the charge. I could not open whichwatts.com (rank 3, uncited) because of an SSL certificate error, so I have not checked it for this point.
decides: This confirms that the plan works only in mild weather. In freezing conditions, a 120 V / 12 A session from any station in the current table (BLUETTI Elite 300, ALLPOWERS R4000 and so on) may add almost no range, because the car's own heater takes the power first. That favours 240 V output, which delivers more power per minute beyond what heating takes: Anker SOLIX F3800 / F3800 Plus EV mode, or Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus with its Grounding Adapter. The rebuilt page should also add a cold-weather caveat to its miles columns. Separately, the current page's 'Level 2 with the $99 adapter' cell for the EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 is wrong. EcoFlow's own FAQ describes the EV X-Stream Adapter as a way to charge the DELTA Pro 3 from EV charging stations, not to charge an EV. That cell has to be removed or corrected.

findings.label: Plugged-in EV uses charger power to warm its battery (maker's words)
findings.value: 'Leave Model S plugged in when not in use. This uses the charging system, rather than the Battery itself, to keep your Battery warm'
findings.source_title: Tesla Model S Owner's Manual, page 90 (Cold Weather Best Practices), via ManualsLib
findings.note: This is a mirror of Tesla's own manual, because tesla.com's ownersmanual pages returned HTTP 403 to my fetch. The manual says a blue snowflake icon means some battery energy is unavailable because the battery is cold. It gives no wattage for battery heating.

findings.label: Share of Level 1 energy stored in a cold battery (named test)
findings.value: 1.14 kWh gained in 14 h at 9 A on 110 V, -15 °F (-26 °C), Tesla Model 3 Long Range AWD; 'only 7% of the power from the outlet actually made it into the battery'; 'roughly 15 kWh' used to keep the battery warm
findings.source_title: A Tesla Model 3 Slow-Charged In -15 Degree Temperatures. Here's How It Went (InsideEVs, Iulian Dnistran, 2025-02-08)
findings.note: The article's figures don't fully agree with each other. At 9 A × 110–120 V × 14 h, the outlet supplied about 13.9–15.1 kWh in total, so '15 kWh warming + 1.14 kWh stored' is a loose statement. Its 65%→70% state of charge would also be more than 1.14 kWh on this pack. Use the 7% / 1.14 kWh claim and attribute it to InsideEVs. My own extrapolation: about 2.05 kWh into the car (Elite 300 row) × 7% ≈ 0.14 kWh ≈ 0.5 mi at 3.5 mi/kWh, and only in comparably extreme cold. The 12 A in our table would help somewhat; InsideEVs says 12 A 'would have made a difference'.

findings.label: Why EV chargers refuse floating-ground power stations (maker's words)
findings.value: Power stations use a 'floating ground'. The charger 'detects the absence of a low-impedance path between the neutral and ground lines', 'interprets this as a ground fault' and 'disengages its internal relay'
findings.source_title: Can a power station charge an electric vehicle (EV)? – Jackery
findings.note: A rival already has this (Jackery is cited by ChatGPT, and ryzzun repeats it).

findings.label: Grounding Adapter compatibility
findings.value: Compatible with HomePower 3600 Pro Max and Explorer 5000 Plus; Explorer 5000 Plus 'must complete a firmware update prior to use'. While the adapter is connected, AC-mains recharging is prohibited and the parallel port is disabled
findings.source_title: Can a power station charge an electric vehicle (EV)? – Jackery
findings.note: The FAQ says 'three models' but names only two. Jackery describes the adapter as 'simulated grounding', not a physical earth connection.

findings.label: EV charging mode and outlet
findings.value: 'Double-press the AC Outlet Button to activate EV mode charging'; 'set the charging rate to less than 25A'; 1× NEMA 14-50 (6,000 W max, 240 V)
findings.note: The page showed the product as 'Sold Out' with no price. It gives no grounding or neutral details for EV use. The same page content covers the F3800 Plus, which lists TT-30 and L14-30 outlets ('EV & RV Charging: Direct charging via NEMA TT-30P or L14-30 ports'), rated 120/240 V, 25 A max.

findings.label: What the EV X-Stream Adapter does
findings.value: It charges the DELTA Pro 3 from EV stations: 'rapid Level 2 charging (240V/2000W) for EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 instead of standard grid power L1 charging rates (120V/2000W) at L2 EV charging stations'
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 FAQ: Everything You Need to Know (EcoFlow US blog, 2025-05-22)
findings.note: The adapter is for input to the power station, so it does not charge an EV. Our current page's DELTA Pro 3 row ('Level 2 with the $99 adapter') misreads this. The FAQ does not mention grounding or neutral.
